title: 5 Young London Collectors Pushing the Scene Forward
summary: What does it mean to collect art in London today? Perhaps the first problem with the question is the idea that there is a single London art world. Across the city, overlapping scenes operate at vastly different scales: artist-run spaces and young galleries sit alongside blue-chip dealers, auction houses, centuries-old collections, and some of the world’s most influential art schools. From Mayfair to Deptford, Fitzrovia to Bethnal Green, art is embedded across London, and there are as many ways into its art world as there are ways to participate in it. For collectors, this vastness creates an unusual proximity to artists and the communities around them. Someone might discover an artist at a graduate show or in a small gallery, follow their work across the city, and support their practice long before institutional or market recognition arrives. Artists, collectors, gallerists, students, curators, and dealers continually move between London’s different art worlds, creating relationships that connect its grassroots scenes to its established institutions and markets. London, 2011 Gilbert & George White Cube This also makes collecting in London amorphous. It can mean buying emerging artists from small galleries, pursuing historic objects through Mayfair dealerships and auction rooms, or simply purchasing a first work to live with at home. While the art market at large still contains its barriers, the sheer breadth of London’s scene offers multiple points of entry, across tastes, generations, communities, and budgets. Perhaps that plurality is what makes collecting in the Big Smoke so distinctive. There is no single route in, no single taste to follow, and no single definition of a collector. Artsy spoke to five collectors about how they navigate London’s overlapping art worlds, what drives them to buy, and the artists, galleries, and institutions that keep them excited about the city. Selim Bouafsoun collects with an international eye For Selim Bouafsoun, collecting is as much about relationships as it is about art. Though his relationship with art began from a young age, it was Alighiero Boetti ’s 2012 retrospective at Tate Modern that proved formative, opening up new ways of thinking about time, collaboration, and systems. Bouafsoun had always wanted to buy art, but initially found the prospect intimidating. Galleries, mentors, and friends eventually gave him the confidence to begin. “Collecting, I’ve come to realise, is never a solitary act,” he told Artsy. His first acquisition was a painting by Bernhard Buhmann , bought from Dubai gallery Carbon12 in November 2015. Today, his collection spans more than 100 artists, with recent acquisitions including Álvaro Barrington , Monia Ben Hamouda , Sebastián Espejo , and Tomasz Kowalski . One work remains particularly close to him: Hommage à Bonnard (1972) by the late Tunisian painter Hédi Turki . In London, Bouafsoun gravitates towards galleries willing to take risks, including Sadie Coles HQ, Carlos/Ishikawa, Emalin, and LBF Contemporary. But he sees some of the city’s greatest energy beyond its established art infrastructure, among artists and spaces operating with limited resources and ambitious ideas. He is particularly excited by an emerging generation shaped by international lives and communities. Their internationalism, he said, “isn’t performed; it’s lived.” Adelle Cohen believes collecting should be for everyone As a new collector, Adelle Cohen’s path into art began, unusually, with being told not to make any. At school, her art teacher would send her into town to buy supplies for the class rather than letting her participate. Her entry into collecting came years later at British artist Shauna Cribbin’s solo show at the Bomb Factory Art Foundation, where an iridescent screenprint on metal caught her attention. “I instantly fell in love and had to buy it,” Cohen recalled. “That’s how I became a collector.” Cohen’s London is centered on galleries in the city’s east, including Maureen Paley, Rose Easton, and Herald St, as well as Harlesden High Street in northwest London. She is drawn to programs that she sees as challenging without becoming exclusionary. That accessibility is central to how Cohen thinks about collecting. Rather than an activity reserved for an established collector class, she believes buying art should be an ordinary way of participating in London’s art scene. “Everyone should be encouraged to buy art,” she said. “We all deserve to own it.” Her taste isn’t entirely bound by seriousness either. The work she currently covets is by Dutch artist Diederik van Apple : an image of Nicolas Cage in the iconic film Leaving Las Vegas printed onto real dollar bills and submerged in glossy resin. “I shouldn’t love it,” Cohen admitted. “But I do.” Fabian Kluth collects through curiosity Fabian Kluth is reluctant to call himself a collector. “I see myself more as a project maker and entrepreneur,” he told Artsy. For him, art is an extension of a broader curiosity about people and what they choose to make. Kluth’s interest in contemporary art intensified during the COVID-19 lockdowns. While galleries and museums were closed, he was struck by how active the art world remained online. Social media became his way into a community he had previously observed from the outside. His first acquisition was a work on paper by German artist Rosa Loy . Since then, Kluth has gravitated towards artists with strong ideas who resist bending their practices to expectations. His collection includes Brett Charles Seiler , Pol Taburet , and Konrad Weichs. He is also drawn to women artists from older generations, including Nan Goldin and the late Swiss painter Irène Zurkinden . In London, Kluth is less interested in the set calendar of fairs and gallery weekends than in accidental discovery. He prefers wandering through the city and entering galleries without a plan, and points to Düsseldorf- and Berlin-based SETAREH ’s Mayfair space as a welcome recent addition. For Kluth, London’s strength lies in its mix of generations and international perspectives. Its art schools are central to that, with Central Saint Martins and the Slade School of Fine Art among the places he looks to for what might come next. Ultimately, his approach starts with people. “Whenever I meet someone,” Kluth said, “one of the first questions I ask is, ‘What are you currently working on?’” Daria Borisova backs artists early For London-based curator and art advisor Daria Borisova, collecting, curating, and community are closely connected. Her work has long centered on emerging artists, and that instinct for discovery carries into her collection: encountering an artist early, for her, is less about predicting the market than supporting a practice as it develops. One of Borisova’s earliest acquisitions was a painting by the late British artist Sarah Cunningham , whom she remembers for the sensitivity and personality of both her work and their interactions. Today, Borisova is drawn to artists developing distinctive ways of working. She points to The Artsy Vanguard alum Emily Kraus , who pulls canvases around constructed rooms to spread and smear paint across their surfaces; KV Duong , whose paintings on latex explore Vietnamese diasporic queer experience; and Antonio Társis , who transforms discarded matchboxes, cardboard, and paint tins into art. “These artists aren’t just making beautiful things,” Borisova said. “They’re making arguments.” Her collection also reflects an appetite for discovering artists early. George Rouy , Eva Helene Pade , Joseph Yaeger, Flora Yukhnovich , and Jadé Fadojutimi are among the artists she encountered before their wider recognition. For Borisova, this process of discovery is central to London’s appeal. Hayward Gallery and the Barbican Centre are favorite institutional haunts, but she sees the city’s real strength in the community around them: collectors, artists, and galleries invested in one another. “The energy starts here,” she said. “We find them first.” Linton Wang looks to the past for inspiration While many young collectors look for the next emerging artist, Linton Wang is more likely to be found pursuing an object several centuries old. His collecting began as a teenager with fountain pens, particularly examples from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Their precious-metal decoration led him towards silver and decorative arts. Studies in history of art, followed by a master’s at the Courtauld Institute, expanded his interests across European art and material culture, with a particular focus on the Age of Enlightenment. For Wang, materiality is non-negotiable. Beauty of form, technical excellence, and fine materials take precedence over concept alone. He is fascinated by objects that have survived for centuries and the lives they have accumulated along the way. “Given one’s own brief existence, to imagine the lives of such works is itself an exercise of the mind,” he said. “Old works have the remarkable ability to grant access to people and ages that had long ceased to exist.” Perhaps unsurprisingly, his favorite London institution is the Wallace Collection, whose French Régence and Louis XV holdings align closely with his own tastes. “I have told myself that should I die without an heir, all my earthly possessions will go to that august institution,” he said. Wang also sees London’s historic art market as very much alive. He values the city’s auction houses for their breadth and accessibility, while its network of specialist dealers maintains a depth of expertise even as traditional dealerships become more private. One of his favorite acquisitions captures the thrill of that market. Wang first encountered an English Chinoiserie silver tea caddy from 1758 at an American auction in 2015, but lost it to another bidder. When it resurfaced a decade later, he bought it. The unknown collector who owned it in between had kept it in pristine condition. The two have never met, but for Wang, their connection through the object reflects the “unspoken camaraderie surrounding a thing of beauty” that makes collecting so compelling.

title: Kiaf SEOUL 2026 announces 175 exhibitors for its 25th edition.
summary: Kiaf SEOUL 2026, Korea’s largest contemporary art fair, has announced 175 exhibitors from 18 countries. Korea’s largest international art fair will return to COEX in Seoul from September 2–6, the same dates and location as Frieze Seoul. Organized by the Galleries Association of Korea, the fair marks its 25th anniversary and, for the first time, has appointed an external creative director: acclaimed designer Kuho Jung, known for his work across fashion, performance, and exhibition design. Jung who will lead the fair’s branding, spatial design, and special exhibition curation. The fair is a central pillar of Seoul Art Week, which connects exhibitions and programs across the city through major institutions including Leeum Museum of Art , Art Sonje Center and Space K. The week also includes district-based evening programs in the city’s gallery districts of Samcheong, Hannam, and Cheongdam. Kiaf SEOUL’s exhibitor list spans established and emerging galleries from Korea and internationally, including first-time participants Nino Mier Gallery and JD Malat Gallery . Returning exhibitors include Korean stalwarts such as Kukje Gallery , Gana Art , and Arario Gallery as well as major international names including Whitestone Gallery and Opera Gallery . The fair will present a mix of historically significant and contemporary works. Korean modern art is well represented, with pieces from Lee Ufan ’s “Wind” series, for example, shown across multiple galleries. Other Korean art highlights include mixed-media works by Dansaekhwa artist Seobo Park at Wellside Gallery, Nam June Paik ’s Internet Dweller wol.five.ydpb (1994) at CMay Gallery , and abstract works by Seund Ja Rhee at Galerie Vazieux. Other major 20th century works on view include a 1982 tempera by Marc Chagall at Art of the World Gallery, Sol LeWitt ’s Irregular Grid (1999) at Obscura Gallery , as well as works by Keith Haring at SH Gallery and David Hockney at Gallery Pici. Kiaf PLUS, the fair’s section for emerging and experimental practices, features eight Korean galleries alongside 11 international participants from Bangkok, Tokyo, New York, Moscow, Taipei, Madrid and Osaka. Kiaf HIGHLIGHTS, an initiative launched in 2023 to support participating artists, returns in an expanded format with dedicated in-booth exhibition spaces, with the aim of offering visitors a more focused viewing experience. Ten artists will be shown at the fair following a jury process led by a panel of art professionals. This year’s edition is themed “Coexistence,” which explores the “evolving relationship between humanity and technology.” Two special exhibitions at the fair expand this. One is entitled “HUMAL”—a portmanteau of “human” and “animal”—and brings together seven interdisciplinary artists examining instinct and embodied perception in an era of artificial intelligence. A second, titled “Invisible,” extends those themes into augmented reality, with AR artworks accessible via QR codes throughout the fair exhibition space.

title: Sculptor Tony Cragg to be awarded the 2026 European Culture Prize.
summary: Sir Tony Cragg will receive the prestigious European Culture Prize 2026, the European Cultural Forum announced. eThe award will be presented on September 4th at the Royal Concertgebouw in Amsterdam. Born in Liverpool in 1949, Cragg has lived and worked in Wuppertal, Germany, since the late 1970s. In 2008, he founded the Waldfrieden Sculpture Park there, which has since grown into one of Europe’s leading sculpture parks and helped establish the city as a destination for contemporary sculpture. “Tony Cragg is one of the most significant sculptors of our time,” said Reiner Schränkler, chairman of the board of the European Cultural Forum. “His works uniquely combine science, nature, materials research and artistic vision. He has had a lasting impact on international sculpture and has inspired generations of artists.” The European Culture Prize, known as TAURUS, was created in 2012 by Dresden artist and European Cultural Forum board member Sven Schubert. The prize rotates annually across categories including music, fine arts, performing arts, environmental protection, and politics. Previous winners have included Gerhard Richter in 2018 and Vivienne Westwood and Neo Rauch in 2019, as well as cellist Sol Gabetta in 2022 and tenor Rolando Villazón in 2024. Felix Krämer, director general and artistic director of the Kunstpalast Düsseldorf, will present Cragg with the award in Amsterdam. Krämer worked with the artist on the 2024 exhibition “Tony Cragg: Please Touch!,” which invited visitors to physically interact with the sculptures on view. This year’s gala, themed “Great Voices–Great Names,” will also honor fashion designer Iris van Herpen , actress Famke Janssen, and violinist Nicola Benedetti, among others, with a concert program built around the honorees’ own performances.

title: An Art Lover’s Guide to Lisbon
summary: In barely a decade, Lisbon has become one of Europe’s most-watched art scenes. The 2011–2014 financial crisis and international bailout left deep bruises across Portuguese society, forcing the city’s cultural milieu to invent new ways of getting by. What followed still caught everyone off guard: An influx of foreign capital—and of the foreigners who bought it—transformed the Portuguese capital, revitalizing its cultural landscape and turning what has long been one of Europe’s most-overlooked art scenes into a fixture of collectors’ itineraries. The change came with costs. “The abundance of cheap spaces that used to exist was great for building a community. Now the problem is you don’t even find that kind of place on the outskirts anymore,” Horácio Frutuoso , artist and Lisbon resident, told Artsy. Today, the city is home to some of Europe’s most-watched galleries, a renewed set of institutions under new leadership, and an independent scene finding its footing amid rapid change. The key neighborhoods for art lovers in Lisbon Estrela Most of the city’s incumbent galleries sit west of Baixa, the historic center, concentrated in or around Campo de Ourique, a comfortably bourgeois district that’s become an anchor of the commercial scene. Galeria São Mamede , founded in 1965, is among the city’s oldest commercial galleries and remains a fixture of the Portuguese scene. Long-established gallerists Cristina Guerra (founded 2001) and Miguel Nabinho (opened 2003) also hold most of the Portuguese scene’s safest bets. Pedro Cera , another Campo de Ourique mainstay credited with real growth in recent years, marked its 25th anniversary by opening a Madrid space and increasingly works with internationally recognised artists. Newer arrivals broker a conversation between local and international markets: Consonni Radziszewski —the new name for Galeria Madragoa, following its 2026 merger with the Warsaw gallery Dawid Radziszewski—now represents artists across spaces in Lisbon, Warsaw, and Milan. Jahn und Jahn , near Jardim da Estrela, opened its first outpost outside Munich here in 2022 and has helped validate Lisbon's scene for foreign collectors, curators, and artists. Just over the border in Rato, Belard has quickly built a reputation for rigorous, no-frills contemporary shows since opening in 2022. Alvalade The tranquil north-central neighborhood was recently jolted by the announced closure of Galeria Vera Cortês , set for 19 December after 23 years in business. But the area still holds solid stalwarts: Quadrado Azul , Balcony , and the Coruchéus complex — a Lisbon City Council-run cluster of 50 artist studios dating to 1971. Nearby is Quadrum gallery tucked into a recess within one of the neighborhood’s residential blocks and Appleton, an independent exhibition space. “We were quite isolated in the Alvalade neighborhood when we opened, and now we’re surrounded. All of this happened in the last 15 years. All these galleries and independent spaces have given the neighborhood strength and made it much more interesting,” Vera Appleton, founder of Appleton , told Artsy. Marvila Further east along the Tagus, Marvila is frequently described as a neighborhood with potential: fewer spaces than Estrela or Alvalade, but well suited to contemporary art thanks to its warehouses and rooms with real scale. dialogue has been singled out as the emerging gallery to watch, praised for establishing itself firmly and running a strong international programme since its first shows around 2023. Francisco Fino , settled since 2017 in a former olive-oil-and-wine warehouse after six itinerant years, has built a roster that has earned steady praise for its work with contemporary artists. The museums and institutions to know in Lisbon Musical chairs at the top of Lisbon’s major museums mean curatorial change has arrived at most of the capital’s key institutions. These reshuffles coincide with major renovations and new arrivals. Calouste Gulbenkian Museum: One of the city’s most beloved institutions reopened in 2026 after 18 months of restoration, timed to coincide with the Gulbenkian Foundation's 70th anniversary. The museum holds the private art collection of oil magnate Calouste Gulbenkian, packed with Egyptian, Greek, and Armenian antiquities and many works from European medieval and Renaissance masters. An unmissable staple is the René Lalique jewelry collection: around 150 Art Nouveau pieces commissioned by Gulbenkian himself and made specifically for him. Centro de Arte Moderna (CAM): Custodian of the largest and most complete collection of modern and contemporary Portuguese art—some 11,700 works by more than 1,300 artists—CAM, part of the Gulbenkian museum complex, inaugurated its Kengo Kuma –designed expansion in 2024, joined by a new 7,515-square-meter garden that gave the city a fresh green counterpart to the Foundation’s original grounds. A recent leadership reshuffle sees Portuguese curator Sergio Mah replacing outgoing director Benjamin Weil; the local expectation is that newer voices will follow. Museum of Contemporary Art and Architecture Centre (MAC/CCB): The leading museum for contemporary art and architecture in Portugal. Unburdened by the once-imposing specter of the collector Joe Berardo—whose sprawling collection is now in the hands of the Portuguese state—MAC/CCB is enjoying a renaissance of sorts. Under artistic director Nuria Enguita, the museum is freer to engage in a more ambitious conversation with Portugal’s recent past and the urgent themes of today. Museu de Arte Contemporânea Armando Martins (MACAM): A private museum attached to a hotel, opened in March 2025 in the restored eighteenth-century Palácio Condes da Ribeira Grande between Alcântara and Belém. Around 200 works from collector Armando Martins’s holdings are on view across some 20,000 square feet. The building’s tiled contemporary extension nods to Portugal’s ceramic tradition. Its programme has helped demystify private collections, and it prides itself on having opened them to public view. Works by the likes of Paula Rego , Amadeo de Souza-Cardoso , and Marina Abramović are among the highlights. Nearby in Alcântara, Ainori Contemporary Art is worth a detour for its emerging-artist programme. Museu do Chiado (MNAC): The country’s first contemporary art museum. Curator Filipa Oliveira, appointed in early 2025, has spoken publicly of wanting Lisbon to fall back in love with the museum. Oliveira has centered her curatorial approach on fostering intergenerational dialogue between Portuguese canon, drawing on the Museum’s extensive collection and contemporary Portuguese art. Works by prominent Portuguese names such as de Souza-Cardoso, Columbano Bordalo Pinheiro, and José de Almada Negreiros are on view. One independent space worth seeking out: messieurs-dames, in the newly hip neighborhood of Penha de França. Founded in 2023, the project space has been singled out for stimulating exhibitions “made by artists for artists,” while keeping a discreet digital profile. Shows here often find dialogues between historical and contemporary art practices, with previous shows featuring artists such as Ana Jotta , Bruno Cidra , and António Palolo . “One part that interests me is this historical and archival side. Projects that were abandoned, that were never shown or never had the conditions to be shown,” founder Eva Mendes told Artsy. A few minutes away in Arroios, Kolibri (formerly Casa Oxente) has built a name for itself with emerging, material-driven work. Where the art world in Lisbon eats, drinks, and shops The places where Lisbon’s art world actually gathers are less concentrated than in most European cities, spread between Bairro Alto, Campolide, and the outer neighborhoods. Click the Google Maps entries to save them to your itinerary. For drinks For drinks The bar at Galeria Zé dos Bois (ZDB) , a nonprofit art center founded in 1994 and a doyen of Bairro Alto, retains its capacity to draw a distinct crowd to a neighborhood under heavy pressure from overcrowding. Cosmos , running since 2020 in a building owned by the 96-year-old sports club Campolide Atlético Clube, is a magnet for everything creative in the city —and one of the few consensus picks among the local milieu. Initially a temporary project during the pandemic years, Casa Capitão will open a permanent space in September; an interdisciplinary venue in the neighborhood of Beato that is also an unmissable hangout. For dinner Near Belém’s museum cluster, and a stone’s throw from contemporary art museum MAAT, restaurant Canalha —with its open kitchen, fresh produce on display, and Iberian culinary influences—has become a local institution since opening in 2023. The tiny neo- tasca (tavern) O Velho Eurico , in Alfama, took on the singular project of reviving the tradition of the classic tasca in a modern setting (the Alfama area is also home to Perve Galeria , one of the city’s oldest spaces devoted to Global South contemporary art). Reservations are recommended; expect long waiting-lists but delicious, unassuming takes on Portuguese dishes. And Galeto , open since 1966, remains a comfort spot for Lisbon dwellers—1960s counter, traditional service, and night-owl-friendly hours. For lunch A few meters from Museu do Chiado/MNAC, in the heart of the Chiado neighborhood, Viennese café Kaffeehaus has been a stalwart of consistency in Lisbon’s center since 2008, keeping the same Austrian classicsf—Sachertorte, Schnitzel​, sausages—on its menu. Midway between Belém and Marvila, on the riverfront, right by Santa Apolónia train station, lies Casanova , another Lisbon classic with an unbeatable view, extensive outside seating, and an unbeatable thin-crust truffle pizza. For browsing Tucked beneath the 25 de Abril Bridge, the art center LX Factory keeps its status intact as a Lisbon favorite 18 years after its opening, still bustling with galleries, cafés, restaurants, and shops. Among Lisbon bookshops, local favorites are Livraria da Travessa , a branch of the namesake bookshop in Rio de Janeiro, and Good Company , an independent bookshop with lots worth reading in the English language. Also much worth visiting is STET ​ , a bookshop and cultural association ​in the Arroios neighborhood, specializing in photography books, artist’s books, and author editions, both Portuguese and international​, with the odd piece from local designers also for sale. Where to stay An inevitable recommendation: MACAM Hote l , a 5-star, 64-room property in Lisbon. It’s the hospitality wing of this museum-and-hotel hybrid, allowing guests to enjoy the Armando Martins contemporary art collection up close. Top tips for art lovers visiting Lisbon When to go: Summer is busier than it used to be, but the who’s who of Lisbon’s art world still tends to reserve July and August for holidays. Book a flight for April through June, when the scene is at full tilt. How to navigate: Lisbon’s known for being a hilly city, but it’s very walkable in the flat areas by the river (Baixa, Belém, Marvila)​. Chiado, despite feeling central, actually sits on a hill above Baixa, not by the Tagus, and is better reached by metro or tram. The compact layout of Portugal’s capital makes reaching other areas, such as Alvalade, easier by metro or bus. Venturing into the steep Estrela neighborhood is best done with the help of trams 28E and 25E​. Uber is cheap, plentiful, and often the easiest way to get around the city. What locals know: Galleries typically open Tuesday through Saturday. Openings, by convention, are usually held in the evening on weekdays, though scheduling—and the ambience of the openings themselves—tends to be fairly informal. Many start as early as late afternoon, often between 7 p.m. and 9 p.m., or sometimes on Saturday afternoons.

title: Elaine de Kooning’s JFK portrait series to go on view in New York this fall.
summary: A major exhibition of Elaine de Kooning ’s work will open at Berry Campbell Gallery in New York on October 29th, spanning four decades of the Abstract Expressionist ’s career from 1948 to 1988. It is the first major solo presentation of her work since the National Portrait Gallery ’s 2015–2016 exhibition “Elaine de Kooning: Portraits,” and many of the works, including paintings and works on paper, have not been shown publicly since the artist’s death. Among the highlights are paintings from De Kooning’s John F. Kennedy series, made after she was commissioned in 1962 to paint an official presidential portrait for the Harry S. Truman Library. The artist was given access to Kennedy during his winter stays in Palm Beach, Florida, in late 1962 and early 1963, but found that his constant motion—reading papers, taking calls, shifting in his chair—made a conventional single sitting impossible. Instead, she worked from rapid sketches, later telling ARTnews that she required “absolute immobility of the sitter,” which the president rarely gave her. By her own account, published in Life magazine in 1964, the process ultimately produced “hundreds of sketches and 23 finished paintings.” Kennedy’s assassination in November 1963 halted her work on the series; she later described the year she’d spent painting him as “real trauma.” The exhibition will also include California (1958–1960), an 11-foot-wide abstraction that ranks among the largest she ever painted, and Bacchus #20-G (1983), part of a series inspired by Jules Dalou ’s 19th-century bronze The Triumph of Silenus in Paris’s Jardin du Luxembourg. An earlier interest in motion appears in Scrimmage (Basketball #3) (1948). Portraits on view include Alex Katz II (1967), Kaldis #12 (1978), depicting her friend and fellow 8th Street Club member Aristodimos Kaldis, and Toni #2 (Toni Ross) (1982), a portrait of the artist she mentored. De Kooning was a founding member of the 8th Street Club and one of 11 women included in the landmark 1951 Ninth Street Show , part of a generation of women later dubbed the “Ninth Street Women” whose contributions to Abstract Expressionism have undergone renewed scholarly attention in recent years. De Kooning also worked as an art critic for ARTnews , helping introduce the movement to wider audiences. The show will follow the Speed Art Museum’s “Abstract Expressionists: The Women,” on view in Louisville, Kentucky, through August, which similarly reexamines the movement’s women artists and counts Berry Campbell among its supporters. The exhibition is accompanied by a 98-page catalogue featuring memoirs by art dealer Arlene Bujese, De Kooning’s goddaughter Denise Lassaw, and artist Toni Ross, along with a biography by Aliza Edelman, Ph.D.

title: How to Craft the Perfect Home Gallery Wall
summary: Gallery Wall #4-Drawing, 2018 Ji Eun Kim Gallery SoSo Few tasks are as simultaneously exciting and daunting for a collector as hanging a home gallery wall, especially for the first time. Gallery walls, also known as salon walls, are a popular way of hanging groups of artworks. Rather than centering a single painting on a wall, gallery walls hang several works in a clustered arrangement ranging from a handful of works to well over a dozen. But where to start? You’ve done the fun part and found and purchased a few artworks you love . You may have even had them framed. Now, you find yourself staring down a blank wall and wondering where on earth to begin. At the back of your mind, there may be a nagging sense that there is a right way to do this. First, take a deep breath and know you’re not alone. The fact is, crafting the perfect gallery wall is not a one-size-fits-all affair, which is part of what makes it an art in itself. “There are no absolute rules when it comes to hanging art,” said Hirofumi Miyauchi, dealer at Andecian Gallery . “Trying to achieve perfection in the absence of rules can feel overwhelming precisely because of that absolute freedom.” Still, interior designers, dealers, and artists all agree that there are some genuinely useful tips and tricks to crafting the gallery wall of your dreams. The biggest hurdle might be learning how to trust your own eye. If hanging a gallery wall has been on your agenda, don’t shy away. We’ve consulted the experts and put together a step-by-step guide to demystifying the process, setting you—and your art—up for success. Start with the wall, not the art Window Watcher 1,2,3 (Triptych), 2020 Robert Pokorny aous Choosing the wall you want to display art on before picking the art itself might seem like putting the cart before the horse, but trust the process. The wall is your canvas, and you can work backwards from there. When selecting a wall, you’ll want to consider the dimensions, how light moves across it through the day, and what furniture sits below it. These constraints can become useful guideposts for selecting the right works. But this is an art, not a science, so don’t get too bogged down in specifics. “There isn’t really a strict rule for the ideal wall, except perhaps to favor the walls your eye is naturally drawn to when you enter a room,” said Sandra Benhamou, a Paris-based art collector and furniture and interior designer. Benhamou is not one to shy away from surprising spaces either. She encourages collectors to think about “hanging a work in an unexpected place, giving a forgotten corner or passageway a new purpose.” Her one suggestion, however, is to avoid walls that face direct sun throughout the day, which could bleach paper works and photographs over time. Some sunlight, however, should be embraced, not eschewed. Gallerists and artists Nicky and Rob Carter, who run the London gallery space RNat5A , say “changing daylight is absolute magic” for art. In their dining room, they note that the shifting sun transforms the mood throughout the day. How to choose artworks that belong together When hanging a gallery wall, it can be wise to unlearn the impulse to make things match. Too much sameness can feel forced and stale. Instead, invite the possibility for unexpected discovery between seemingly dissimilar works. “Don’t be afraid to place pieces together that may seem unrelated, whether in style, value, or historical importance,” said Benhamou. “A modest work can become incredibly noble when it finds its rightful place, and a masterpiece doesn’t need to be surrounded by other masterpieces or occupy the center of the wall to shine.” Others put it more bluntly. “Never match your art to your soft furnishings,” said Rob and Nicky Carter. “Works go together simply because you chose them,” they add. Mohamed Benhadj, gallery director and curator at Al-Tiba9 gallery in Barcelona, encourages collectors to find relationships between works that are intellectual rather than visual. “A strong gallery wall is usually connected by the idea that relates each piece to another,” he said. That shouldn’t be confined to mediums, either, he adds: “Don’t be afraid to combine painting, photography, and prints.” Miyauchi, meanwhile, suggests mixing several arrangements until something clicks visually. “Hanging multiple paintings could be compared to a chord in music,” he said. “An unexpected combination might beautifully come together.” He encourages collectors not to over-intellectualize the process to start. “It is more than enough to look at books or the internet and simply imitate what somehow catches your fancy,” he added. Thinking about scale, spacing, and arrangement Gathering, 2026 Allison Gildersleeve Upsilon Gallery When placing works together in a group, the frames don’t need to match each other. But they should suit each individual artwork. “I don’t believe a frame should ever be separated from the artwork it belongs to,” Benhamou said. “It should reflect the work’s format, medium, and period.” The Carters agree. “Frame the artwork, not the room.” Benhadj, who mixes finishes within his own collection—for example, thin natural wood on a set of drawings, a minimalist black frame on a large print, and an ornate gilt frame on a modern oil painting—recommends anchoring variety with one dominant style so the wall gains character without becoming too visually noisy. “I enjoy seeing different frame styles when there is a clear intention behind the selection,” he added. How to know when to stop Aura of an Interior, 2023 Degard Visionary British Museum Knowing when a gallery wall is complete is both subjective and essential. Benhamou tells collectors not to rush to conclusions. “The most beautiful arrangements evolve over time, just like the collection itself,” she said. The Carters offer a simpler test: “You stop when it stops making you smile.” A gallery wall, experts agree, is never truly permanent. Pieces can move, rotate, and rest until their moment comes back around. Miyauchi even encourages collectors to rotate artworks over time. “I recommend changing your paintings on special days, such as the summer and winter solstices, birthdays, or Christmas,” he said. “You change them just like you would open a window to let fresh air into a room. The paintings you take down can rest until the timing is right for them again.” All the experts believe that one key to crafting the perfect gallery wall is leaving it open to the possibilities of the future. As Benhadj puts it, “what connects well on a particular wall today might connect even better with works that become part of their collection in the next 5 or 10 years.” A gallery wall that feels slightly too today, he said, can be an invitation to discover what’s next.

title: Meet the Italian Shoe Designer Who Collects Art by Andy Warhol, Barbara Kruger, and More
summary: Walk into a church in Naples, Italy, and you might stumble across a Caravaggio or an Artemisia Gentileschi . For Italian shoe designer and collector Ernesto Esposito, that proximity to beauty shaped everything that followed. “I grew up in Naples, a city where beauty is not confined to museums but is part of everyday life,” Esposito said. “Art came first. Long before becoming a shoe designer, I was already fascinated by beauty, proportions, and the emotional power of objects.” Esposito began his career in the 1970s with renowned shoemaker Sergio Rossi. His own collections pair classic silhouettes with more daring designs, including towering open-toe heels in leopard-print pony hair and red patent leather. Over several decades, he has also built an art collection featuring works by Katharina Grosse , Richard Prince , John Baldessari , Andy Warhol , Joseph Beuys , Cindy Sherman , Barbara Kruger , and George Condo , alongside those by younger painters such as Leonardo Devito and Adam Handler . For Esposito, collecting is not simply about ownership, taste, or market value. It is a way of living with questions, memories, friendships, and creative risk. Starting with Warhol His first acquisition was a limited-edition silkscreen from Warhol’s 1971 “ Electric Chair ” series. “I did not choose it because it was fashionable, nor as an investment,” he said. “I bought it because it moved me deeply. It is a work that is at once beautiful, unsettling, and profoundly human.” That instinct has guided him ever since. “Great art does not provide answers, but instead asks questions that continue to stay with you throughout your life,” he said. “That work defined the direction of my entire collection.” Growing up amid Naples’s layered history taught Esposito that objects could carry meaning beyond their function. “When I became a designer, I never considered a shoe to be merely a product,” he said. “To me, a shoe is a cultural object, capable of expressing identity, emotion, and creativity.” He sees a direct connection between art and fashion. “All of my work in fashion has always been guided by the same curiosity and sensitivity that first made me fall in love with art,” he said. Esposito also resists a simple distinction between craftsman and artist. “Great craftsmen possess artistic sensitivity, while great artists often have extraordinary mastery of technique,” he said. “Excellence is always born from the meeting of imagination and skill.” Building an art collection of sensibilities What unifies his collection is not a theme or medium, but a sensibility. “I am drawn to artists who possess an authentic and recognizable language,” he said. “I do not collect a particular style, but rather personalities.” His approach was shaped in part by the legendary Neapolitan dealer and curator Lucio Amelio. “Meeting Lucio opened an entirely new world to me,” Esposito said. “Through him, I met extraordinary artists and discovered that art does not simply serve to decorate a space, but can change the way we look at and understand reality.” Collecting, he said, then became “an integral part of the way I live and interpret the world.” For Esposito, buying art requires conviction. “A true collector is someone who takes responsibility,” he said. “They choose according to their own instinct, not according to market consensus.” One artist currently holding his attention is De Vito. Esposito admires “the consistency of his research, the quality of his painterly language, and his ability to address contemporary themes without chasing trends.” Following a young artist’s development, he added, “is one of the most fascinating aspects of collecting.” Collecting emerging and established artists alongside each other Little Runner Abduction, 2026 Adam Handler Trium Art Gallery He refuses to rank emerging talent against established masters. “The great masters represent the memory and history of art, while emerging artists bring energy, freedom, and unpredictability,” he said. In a market saturated with spectacle, sincerity still moves him most. “The works that truly stay with us are those still capable of conveying a personal truth,” he said. “Authenticity remains the rarest quality.” Art’s influence on his footwear is rarely literal. “Sometimes it is a color combination, other times a proportion, or perhaps the courage to make an unexpected decision,” he said. “The influence of art is constant, often unconscious, but always present.” Designing and collecting may appear to arise from the same impulse, but Esposito experiences them differently. “Designing allows me to create. Collecting allows me to listen,” he said. “When I design, I am the one making decisions. When I collect, I enter into dialogue with someone else’s vision.” His most recent direct collaboration was a residency with American painter Adam Handler. Handler reminded him of a young Keith Haring , whom Esposito met in New York early in Haring’s career. “It is not a stylistic comparison,” Esposito said, “but rather the energy, enthusiasm, and total dedication to work that I recognized again in Adam.” Staged with Trium Art Gallery in Monza, Italy, and Noh-Art , the residency became more than a commission. Esposito credited Naples—its light, history, energy, and openness—with transforming it into “something far deeper than a simple artistic collaboration.” “The work itself is certainly important, but what truly remains is the experience shared together,” he said. “Artists need places capable of inspiring them, authentic encounters, and human relationships.” Looking ahead, Esposito imagines future residencies with artists chosen not for their market standing, but for their openness: “an artist capable of being surprised by Naples just as much as Naples could be surprised by them.” It is from that encounter, he believes, that “the most authentic projects can emerge.”

title: Artist Betye Saar dies at 99.
summary: Artist Betye Saar , whose assemblages transformed ephemera and heirlooms into meditations on Black history, racism, memory, and spirituality, died in her sleep on July 26 in Los Angeles, four days before her 100th birthday. Her death was confirmed by Roberts Projects , the Los Angeles gallery that represented her for close to two decades. “Betye Saar was one of the greatest artists of our time, and it has been an immense honor to work with her for nearly 20 years,” Julie Roberts, co-founder of Roberts Projects, said in a statement. “Her singular vision transformed the course of contemporary art, and her legacy will continue to inspire generations of artists, scholars, and audiences around the world.” Born Betye Irene Brown in Los Angeles in 1926, Saar was the eldest of three children of Jefferson Maze Brown and Beatrice Lillian Parson. Her father died when she was about five, and her mother moved the family to Pasadena to live with a maternal aunt, Hattie Parson Keys, whose belongings later inspired a series of assemblages made in her honor. Saar spent summers at her paternal grandparents’ home in the Watts neighborhood in L.A., watching artist Simon Rodia construct his monumental architectural sculpture Watts Towers by hand, inspiring Saar’s passion for using found and repurposed materials. Saar studied design at UCLA and worked for years as an interior decorator, at one point running a studio called Brown and Tann with fellow designer Curtis Tann. In 1952, she married ceramicist Richard Saar; the couple settled in Laurel Canyon, Hollywood Hills, and had three daughters, Lezley, Alison , and Tracye, before divorcing in the late 1960s. Saar remained in the Laurel Canyon house for the rest of her life. The Long Memory, 1998 Betye Saar CLAMP Her turn toward fine art came almost by chance. Enrolled at Cal State Long Beach to pursue a teaching credential, Saar wandered into the printmaking studio and immediately changed course. “The move into fine art, it was liberating,” she later told the Los Angeles Times . “It gave me freedom to experiment.” Her early prints carried mystical and occult overtones, drawn from books on alchemy and palmistry, and she began framing them in old window frames scavenged from junk shops. A 1967 exhibition of Joseph Cornell ’s boxed assemblages at the Pasadena Art Museum pushed Saar toward three dimensions. In 1969, she completed Black Girl’s Window , built around a salvaged window frame layering autobiographical imagery, astrology, and racial identity. Trips to Chicago’s Field Museum, where she immersed herself in African art, and to Haiti in the early 1970s, where she explored voodoo and folk magic, further shaped her visual language. Saar’s best-known work, The Liberation of Aunt Jemima (1972), transformed a stereotypical “mammy” figurine—armed with a rifle and grenade—into what she described as a warrior against servitude. First shown at the Rainbow Sign, a Black cultural center in Berkeley, California, near the headquarters of the Black Panthers, the piece connected Saar to the Black Arts Movement and led to a solo exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art in 1975. Activist Angela Davis later credited it with helping to spur the Black women’s movement. “I wanted to empower her,” Saar said in a 2015 interview . “I wanted to make her a warrior.” The original assemblage now belongs to the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive . 4 Doors in a Window (Bellagio, Italy - 1994), 2004 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Over the following decades, Saar continued mining flea markets, yard sales, and family heirlooms, producing works including Records for Hattie (1975), Mojotech (1987), and the altarpiece Wings of Morning (1992), alongside installations like House of Fortune (1988). Scholar Kellie Jones, who curated the 2011 exhibition “Now Dig This! Art and Black Los Angeles 1960–1980” at the Hammer Museum , said in a TK that Saar’s reach extended well beyond the U.S.: “She has works with Mexican milagros, she has titles in Spanish, she at certain points has Asian influence and Haitian influence... She was a person in the world.” Her practice inspired a generation of artists, including her daughter, the artist Alison Saar. Saar’s work is held in the collections of more than 80 institutions worldwide, and she had solo exhibitions at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, the Fondazione Prada in Milan, as well as the Los Angeles County Museum of Art and the California African American Museum. “I’ve always done what I did and never felt I was competing with what was going on,” she told the Los Angeles Times of her career. She continued working into her late 90s, including a commissioned installation at the Huntington Library’s gardens, made at 96 and now on view as “Betye Saar: Drifting Toward Twilight” through November 2027. “Even in death those things can be really beautiful,” she said of the installation in an accompanying documentary. Two other shows remain on view during her centennial year: “ Let’s Get It On: The Wearable Art of Betye Saar ” at Roberts Projects, in Los Angeles, through August 22, and “Betye Saar’s Black Dolls” at the New York Historical Society, through October 4. Her works are currently included in “ Tarot! Renaissance Symbols, Modern Visions ” at the Morgan Library & Museum. Saar is survived by her daughters, Lezley Saar, Alison Saar, and Tracye Saar-Cavanaugh, as well as six grandchildren, including the artist Maddy Inez , and a pet tortoise named Rojo. Her artistic legacy is now overseen by the Betye Saar Legacy Group , a coalition of scholars and curators the artist assembled in 2025 with Roberts Projects. A biography by Zoé Whitley, co-curator of “Soul of a Nation: Art in the Age of Black Power,” is expected in 2027.

title: Guggenheim Abu Dhabi announces 2026 opening date.
summary: The Guggenheim Abu Dhabi will open to the public on December 11, Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism has announced. First announced in 2006, the museum is one of the most anticipated museum openings in decades. Designed by the late Frank Gehry , the building is defined by ten sculptural cones rising to heights of up to 88 metres. Nine are surrounded by stainless steel mesh, providing natural ventilation and shade while giving the structure its distinctive skyline. Its 30 galleries, across 11,600 square meters of interior space, are connected by a central atrium, with a further 23,000 square meters of outdoor exhibition areas. The total built-up area totals 80,000 square metres, the largest of the four Guggenheim locations. The museum will focus on modern and contemporary art from the 1960s to the present, with a particular emphasis on North Africa, and West and South Asia. Rather than presenting art chronologically, the collection will be organised around thematic and geographic groupings. Among the sections are “Abstractions,” “Popular Culture,” “Land,” and “Language and Storytelling.” The collection has been in development since 2009. Guggenheim Abu Dhabi joins the Guggenheim Foundation’s constellation of museums in New York , Venice , and Bilbao , while maintaining, its organisers say, a distinct identity rooted in the cultural and historical position of the United Arab Emirates. It is located on Saadiyat Island, where several high profile museums have opened in recent years, such as Louvre Abu Dhabi, the Zayed National Museum, Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, and teamLab Phenomena Abu Dhabi . “The Guggenheim Foundation is proud and delighted to be a longstanding partner with the Department of Culture and Tourism –Abu Dhabi in shaping a museum of contemporary art of magnificent scope and aspiration,” said Dr. Mariët Westermann, director and CEO of the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation, in a statement. “The museum’s art collection is uniquely local and global, centered in the region but with works from all continents.”

title: National Portrait Gallery acquires Harley Weir’s portrait of Charli XCX.
summary: The National Portrait Gallery in London has acquired a portrait of pop star Charli XCX by British photographer Harley Weir . The photograph, which was shot in 2024, will be added to the museum’s collection this week. The untitled work shows the singer leaning against a wall in a white crop top and unbuttoned black jeans and is now on view in the gallery’s History Makers Now space, which spotlights figures who have shaped contemporary culture. The image became one of the defining pictures of Charli’s Brat era, the 2024 album that turned her into a mainstream phenomenon on the strength of its candor and “debauched swagger,” as the BBC described it . The acquisition was funded by a gift from the Bukhman Foundation. “Harley Weir has developed a distinctive photographic language that combines intimacy with a powerful sense of presence,” said Brandei Estes, the gallery’s senior curator of photographs. “We are delighted to acquire this striking portrait of Charli XCX, which captures one of the defining cultural figures of her generation.” The acquisition arrives the same week Charli released her eighth album, Music, Fashion, Film , built around chopped-up guitar samples and distorted melodies that find her reflecting on fame and artistic identity in Brat ’s aftermath. Portraits of pop stars have been grabbing headlines recently. In March, the National Portrait Gallery acquired West End Girl (Lily Allen) (2025), a painting by Spanish artist Nieves González that doubled as the cover art for Allen’s album of the same name. Charli herself was previously the subject of a portrait by painter Issy Wood , commissioned for the November 2025 cover of Vanity Fair . Beyond music, Charli has been expanding into film, with recent roles in the Polish drama Erupcja , the ensemble film Sacrifice alongside Anya Taylor-Joy and Chris Evans, and the mockumentary The Moment , based on the release of the Brat album. She is set to headline the Reading and Leeds festivals in the U.K. next month before a North American tour in the fall.

title: Georgia O’Keeffe Ghost Ranch paintings to go on display in the U.K. for the first time in 2027.
summary: The Courtauld Gallery in London will open “ Georgia O’Keeffe : Ghost Ranch” in October 2027, an exhibition of nearly two dozen works that explore how the American artist’s New Mexico property shaped her painting practice. Most of the works have never been exhibited in the U.K., according to the Guardian , which first reported the news. Only six of the roughly two dozen paintings in the exhibition have been previously exhibited in Britain, it revealed. Ghost Ranch, a remote property in the high desert north of Santa Fe, became O’Keeffe’s summer home starting in 1934, when she began renting a room on the 21,000-acre estate before eventually purchasing it. “As soon as I saw it, that was my country,” she once said. “I’d never seen anything like it before, but it fitted to me exactly.” Dr. Karen Serres, senior curator of paintings at the Courtauld, told the Guardian that O’Keeffe’s relationship to Ghost Ranch remains under-recognized in Britain despite its centrality to her work. “Ghost Ranch was such an important part of her life, and it illuminates a large part of her art in general,” Serres said, pointing to works like Red and Yellow Cliffs (1940) and Gerald’s Tree I (1937) as direct responses to the surrounding landscape. The show also arrives against a history of uneven critical reception to O’Keeffe in the U.K. In 1993, a Hayward Gallery exhibition drew dismissive reviews from British critics, and more recently, the reception to her 2016 Tate Modern show was largely framed around disputing assumptions that her flower paintings depicted female genitalia. “She’s known as just this formidable female artist,” said Serres. “But actually seeing her work, understanding what she’s about, I don’t think we are there yet.” The Courtauld exhibition follows a fresh wave of attention to O’Keeffe elsewhere. The Detroit Institute of Arts opens “Georgia O’Keeffe: Architecture” on September 11th, an exhibition of nearly 40 works examining her engagement with the built environment, from Manhattan skyscrapers to New Mexico adobe structures, anchored by Stables (1932), which is owned by the museum. On October 3rd, Hauser & Wirth inaugurates its new Palo Alto gallery with “Calder | O’Keeffe,” the first exhibition devoted to the artist’s decades-long friendship with Alexander Calder , developed with the Calder Foundation and the Georgia O’Keeffe Museum. A documentary about the artist , directed by Academy Award– and Emmy Award–winning filmmakers Paul Wagner and Ellen Casey Wagner, was also released earlier this year.

title: Legendary Gallerist Claes Nordenhake on Artists, Arguments, and 50 Years in the Art Business
summary: “As a young gallerist, I was a cleaner, a security guard, an interiordesigner, a carpenter, a courier, a warehouse manager, and a stock clerk,” said Claes Nordenhake, the Swedish art dealer whose eponymous enterprise, Galerie Nordenhake , celebrates its half-century this year. Over five decades, the business has grown from a modest space opened in 1976 in Malmö on the southern coast of Sweden, showing contemporary art—favoring Minimalist , often conceptual, works—into a powerhouse brand with galleries in Stockholm, Berlin, and Mexico City. Talking to Artsy from his Berlin branch, Nordenhake’s stocktake of his early duties doesn’t end there. Starting out, he was obliged to be a photographer, philosopher, business strategist, psychotherapist, and a divorce counselor, he explained. He could be a “sympathetic drinking buddy” one day and an “arrogant bastard” the next. And, when the occasion allowed, he was an art dealer. Roots in Malmö Nordenhake was born in 1948 and grew up in the Skåne region of southern Sweden, where his family owned several quarries celebrated for their Ebony Black granite—a material highly sought after by artists such as Isamu Noguchi and Max Bill . “Coming from a rather conventional business family, sort of a bourgeois upbringing, the artists that I encountered offered another different view on life,” he noted. And there was art at home. “My old man had a collection of mainly Swedish artists, but at some point, he got absolutely fascinated by Lucio Fontana . He had three paintings: one red, one white, and one blue. Fontana in the 1960s was like the ultimate avant-garde.” Green Felt Piece, 1983-84 Robert Morris Galerie Nordenhake Wandrelief, 1988 Ulrich Rückriem Galerie Nordenhake Nordenhake initially trained as a lawyer but quit his studies to pursue his interest in art. I suggest that Malmö in the 1970s could hardly have been a center of Conceptual art . “No, for sure. But the advantage of Malmö was that it was very close to the rest of Europe,” Nordenhake explained. “I would drive my car, and if I left Malmö in the morning, I would be in Cologne in the afternoon or evening. It would take the same time from Malmö to Stockholm.” He targeted a “cosmopolitan” clientele. “There were maybe five collectors who were interested in international art and wanted to be part of that scene,” he said. “I was convinced of certain things. I was very interested in Concrete art …and I made these few collectors follow my interest.” He kept costs low—“hand to mouth”—and acquired a reputation for showing monochrome paintings by internationally renowned artists such as Robert Mangold , Alan Uglow , and Marcia Hafif , as well as Minimalist sculptures by Robert Morris and Ulrich Rückriem . Closer to home, he championed the work of the Swedish modernist painter Olle Bærtling . “He was absolutely exceptional,” recalled Nordenhake. “He was working with colors that, I mean…the blue would never be the blue of the sky, the green never the green of the grass. They were sorts of fields of energy.” How Nordenhake expanded its footprint The business moved to Stockholm in the mid-1980s, when Nordenhake was offered a “sensational space” in the Royal Academy of Fine Arts building. “I’m sure there were a lot of discussions in the gallery about whether one should let the enemy into the house?” he said, laughing, referring to the inclusion—or contamination—of a commercial gallery in a museum context. The rooms allowed him to present larger sculptures, including works by Richard Serra . In 2000 he opened in Berlin, when the city had become a magnet for both artists and gallerists taking advantage of the low rents for studios and a sense of zeitgeist. “I thought it would have been easier,” he recalled. “It was an experiment to come with three kids and my wife and move the entire family. I come from a shit-kicking little town in southern Sweden, so I have no experience of big cities.” At the time, Berlin’s reputation as an artistic hotbed following the fall of the Wall was more than a cliché, said Nordenhake, at least to begin with. “From 1990 to 2010, even a young artist could find an apartment and a studio rather easily,” Nordenhake said. Collectors would visit from abroad to experience the scene. Rents rose over the subsequent years, and the tone shifted. But Nordenhake has helped to foster a collegiate atmosphere among the city’s galleries. In 2005, he co-founded (with Max Hetzler) the first Gallery Weekend Berlin , which, two decades later, now includes some 50 participating galleries and has become a template copied in major cities around the world. Nordenhake opened a third gallery in 2018 in Mexico City, on the suggestion of his former intern, Toni Sadurní Viñas (the gallery’s current director). “Mexico City is the new Berlin,” he declared. “ At the beginning of this century and until recently, Berlin was a place where artists, even young artists, could afford both a studio and an apartment. Which is still the case in Mexico City.” And, he noted, the general public appreciates its artistic heritage, “from the pre-Columbian artifacts to Frida Kahlo and the muralists. Art means something for Mexicans.” Lessons from 50 years in the art trade Is it easy to work with artists over a long period? “I would say usually no. But of course, there are always exceptions,” he smiled. The artist-gallerist relationship is similar to a “marriage,” he said, with all the “conflicts” that implies. And being a gallerist is a work in progress. “You learn stuff,” he noted, adding that his opinion on artists’ work can change over time. “I’m much more generous than I used to be. My art world has gotten bigger.” “Contemporary art is a notoriously slippery commodity in which to do business,” said Philip Hook, author of Rogues’ Gallery, a History of Art and its Dealers . “Very few art dealers remain at the forefront of the avant-garde beyond one generation.” Claes’s son, Sten, is now a director at Galerie Nordenhake, offering a future path for a gallery that needs exceptional mental and commercial agility to continue interpreting the ever-changing new. This is illustrated by the gallery’s 50th anniversary group exhibitions, staged across its three locations, showing artists from its past and present roster, from Bærtling’s last known painting, Ksard (1980), to newly commissioned works by Lap-See Lam (winner of the prestigious Lise Wilhelmsen Art Award last year). And while he is aware of the challenges—both commercially and intellectually—Nordenhake stated that “curiosity is the most amazing driving force. I’m a traveling salesman and a schoolteacher.” Just two more professions to add to his list.

title: 7 Unforgettable Art Day Trips Worth Taking in Summer 2026
summary: Summer 2026 is in full swing, and it’s been an exciting one so far, with highlights ranging from the FIFA World Cup to The Odyssey . But as we enter the quieter phase of the season, your calendar might be a little more open, making it the perfect time to add an art excursion to your summer agenda. Though some art acolytes will certainly be venturing to visit the Venice Biennale 2026 , by and large, the summer is a sleepier season for the art world’s major cities. It’s thus a good time of year to get off the beaten path and take a detour. Day trips, by car, train, or ferry, are an easy way to experience art at a slower, more focused pace. We’ve put together a list of seven standout institutions reachable from major cities—all accessible with little effort. At each of these destinations, you’ll find idyllic settings, world-class architecture, and unforgettable art. This summer, there are can’t-miss exhibitions on view, too, from Issy Wood ’s first Nordic museum show at the Kistefos Museum in Norway to Anicka Yi ’s first large-scale outdoor project at Storm King in upstate New York. Instituto Inhotim Brumadinho, Minas Gerais, Brazil Getting there: About an hour away by car from Belo Horizonte, Brazil, served by Confins International Airport. Wander the sprawling open-air museum and gardens of Brazil’s Instituto Inhotim as birds fly overhead and tropical plants provide a canopy of green. Founded in 2004 by collector Bernardo Paz and set in the verdant hills of Minas Gerais, Instituto Inhotim opened to the public in 2006. There is no place else quite like it. Occupying over 5,000 acres, the institute is both a nature preserve, home to over 1,000 plant species, and a singular art venue encompassing sculpture gardens and close to two dozen galleries showing both permanent collection and temporary exhibitions. Currently, over 900 works by 50 artists are on view. Inhotim turns 20 in 2026, and it’s marking the anniversary with new site-specific commissions as well as with the return of The Murder of Crows (2008), Janet Cardiff and George Bures Miller ’s 98-speaker sound installation later this fall. These will be on view alongside works by Cildo Meireles , Doris Salcedo , Matthew Barney , and Hélio Oiticica , among others. Storm King Art Center New Windsor, New York Getting there: About 90 minutes from New York City by car, or by Metro-North train plus a shuttle. Less than two hours from the hubbub of midtown Manhattan lies Storm King, a 500-acre sculpture park situated on rolling meadows. Here, one can easily spend a day wandering on foot, discovering monumental sculptures and installations around every corner. Among the perennial highlights are Maya Lin ’s rolling hill Storm King Wavefield (2009), Alexander Calder ’s towering red steel Five Swords (1976) , and Menashe Kadishman ’s Suspended (1977), which is among the center’s most popular photo ops. Opened to the public in 1960, the pioneering outdoor space continues to embrace contemporary art with yearly temporary exhibitions. The 2026 season brings Anicka Yi’s first large-scale outdoor project, an installation of towering acrylic columns filled with organic matter set into a seven-acre field. Also on view are artist Saif Azzuz ’s steel-and-salvage sturgeon and artist Liz Glynn ’s concrete casts of Gilded Age furniture. For ambitious art lovers, the trip can be paired with a visit to Dia Beacon, 20 minutes away across the river, for a combination of outdoor and indoor Minimalist and land art in a single trip. The 2026 season runs through November 9th. Kistefos Museum Jevnaker, Norway Getting there: About an hour’s drive or express bus from Oslo. As visitors approach, the Kistefos Museum’s building is likely to stop visitors dead in their tracks. Set along the Randselva river, the stunning museum, designed by the Bjarke Ingels Group, is known as “The Twist.” The massive building, glass at one end, folded aluminum on the other, represents just that, twisting its horizontal form across the length of the river. At once a gallery, a sculpture, and a bridge, the structure is an architectural destination in its own right. But that’s just the start. The museum is home to a sculpture park built around a 19th-century wood-pulp mill (old machinery is still visible, as is timber and turbines). Currently, more than 50 outdoor works are located along the riverbank and surrounding forest; these include a new 13-ton bronze by Dana Schutz , her largest work to date. A new Marguerite Humeau commission will be arriving this fall. This year, museum exhibitions are also noteworthy. Issy Wood ’s first major exhibition in the Nordic region, titled “Fish, Fish, Duck,” is currently on view. The show brings together a selection of Wood’s seductive and restrained compositions that draw from the internet, advertising, auction catalogues, and popular culture to create uneasy images that tap into questions of desire and power. Noah Purifoy Outdoor Desert Art Museum Joshua Tree, California Getting there: About two hours from Los Angeles by car. The site is unstaffed, so visit during daylight and bring water. For those who want an unmediated art experience in the American desert, the Noah Purifoy Outdoor Desert Art Museum is an ideal destination. At an unmarked turnoff on a dirt road in the Mojave Desert lies a sprawling 10-acre sculpture park with works made of bicycle parts, television sets, toilets, and salvaged wood. The American artist Noah Purifoy moved out there in 1989 and spent the last 15 years of his life building the site alone. Purifoy is considered the father of the West Coast assemblage movement. He was influenced in part by the found debris he began working with after the 1965 Watts riot. After decades in Los Angeles, he created the museum as his final and largest body of work. The sprawling work was nearly bulldozed in 2001 before a foundation of his friends stepped in to preserve it. The site is free to visit. There are no tickets or explanatory texts. It’s an increasingly rare opportunity for a raw encounter with an artist’s unadulterated vision at such a scale. Museum SAN Wonju, South Korea Getting there: Roughly 90 minutes to 2 hours from Seoul by car, bus, or train. A car or taxi is recommended for the final stretch to the museum. Located in the Oak Valley, a resort in Gangwon Province, Museum SAN opened in 2013, a space where art and nature could commune. The museum’s name is an acronym, which stands for “space, art, nature.” Today, the museum is one of Korea’s most significant private museums, welcoming hundreds of thousands of visitors every year. Designed by Pritzker Prize–winning Japanese architect Tadao Ando , the museum is an elegant concrete-and-glass structure that seems to emerge from the terrain. Adding to the serene effect are a reflecting pool, a stone garden, and a flower field planted in concentric rings on the grounds. Ando’s relationship with the museum has continued over a decade, with the architect subsequently contributing the Meditation Hall (2018) and Space of Light (2023). In 2025, he revealed his newest structure, Ground , an arched concrete chamber conceived with British artist Antony Gormley , whose works are on view inside. Remarkably, five James Turrell works— Sky Space , Horizon Room , Ganzfeld , Wedgework , and Space Divisio n —are also on permanent view at the museum. But beyond these Turrell environments , the museum has a prominent collection, with a distinct focus on paper artworks ranging from hanji crafts to paper books and everything in between. Glenstone Museum Potomac, Maryland Getting there: Glenstone is about an hour from Washington, D.C., or Baltimore. Admission is free, but timed tickets must be booked online in advance. Glenstone is only 15 miles from downtown Washington, D.C., but it feels a world away. Situated on rolling hills, the museum is a tranquil and contemplative space founded to be a space where art, architecture, and landscape are considered a single work. This year, Glenstone celebrates its 20th year with a host of programming and talks focused on everything from Jeff Koons ’s Split-Rocker (2000) (perhaps the museum’s most iconic work) to the architecture of Charles Gwathmey , who designed Glenstone’s original museum buildings (later expansions by Thomas Phifer and Partners are also marvelous). Also on view are special exhibitions including “ Andrea Bowers, ” an exhibition that brings together over 40 works by the American artist, making it one of the largest exhibitions of Bowers’ work to date. Muzeum Susch Susch, Switzerland Getting there: Susch is just over two hours from Zürich by car or train. In a fairytale-like village of the Swiss Alps lies Muzeum Susch, a museum housed in what once was a medieval monastery and 19th-century brewery. The museum, which opened in 2018, is the project of Polish art collector and philanthropist Grażyna Kulczyk and offers a one-of-a-kind art-viewing experience. The museum is primarily focused women artists, and artworks that focus on matrilineal histories and overlooked histories. Muzeum Susch has more than a dozen permanent installations on view, many site-specific, by artists including Tracey Emin , Monika Sosnowska , and Magdalena Abakanowicz . On view now is “Unraveling,” the first major retrospective of the mid-20th-century Italian artist and activist Mariuccia Secol, tracing seven decades of a practice that moved from painting into aprons, metal scouring pads, and a wedding dress dismantled by hand, a powerful commentary on domestic labor.

title: The New York Knicks’ NBA championship trophy to be displayed at the American Museum of Natural History.
summary: The NBA's iconic Larry O’Brien Championship Trophy, newly engraved with the New York Knicks' championship win, is getting a museum moment. The championship award is going on view at the American Museum of Natural History (AMNH), as part of the exhibition “ For the Win: Objects of Sports Excellence .” The trophy will be unveiled at the museum on July 27th. “For the Win” will be on view through January 3, 2027. Designed by Tiffany & Co. , the trophy depicts a regulation-size basketball entering a net, cast in sterling silver with gold vermeil and weighing about 30 pounds. It bears the name of every NBA champion since 1947 and takes its name from Larry O’Brien, who served as the league’s commissioner from 1975 to 1984. The trophy’s arrival marks a full-circle moment for “For the Win,” which opened in May. Among its roughly 70 objects—spanning 15 sports and nearly 150 years of athletic history—is a basketball-shaped fob presented to former Knicks head coach Red Holzman after the team’s 1973 championship, its last before this year’s win. “When we opened ‘For the Win,’ Red Holzman’s 1973 Knicks championship fob was the piece that connected this city to its basketball past,” said guest curator Vikki Tobak in a statement. “Now the NBA’s Larry O’Brien Trophy arrives with the Knicks’ names freshly engraved on it, and that circle closes in a way we never could have planned.” AMNH president Sean M. Decatur framed the trophy’s arrival as part of a broader moment. “This championship has given New Yorkers an extraordinary moment to celebrate together,” he said, calling the trophy “a powerful symbol of athletic achievement.” Other highlights in “For the Win” include one of Jesse Owens’s gold medals from the 1936 Berlin Olympics , the NFL’s Vince Lombardi Trophy, and the New York Liberty’s 2024 WNBA championship trophy. Tobak curates the exhibition in partnership with Rich Kleiman, the CEO of the sports entertainment company Boardroom, and with Kate Kiseeva, associate curator in the Museum’s Division of Physical Sciences.

title: MFA Boston to host exclusive U.S. Pierre-Auguste Renoir exhibition in February 2027.
summary: Dance at Le Moulin de la Galette (Bal du moulin de la galette), 1876 Pierre-Auguste Renoir Musée d'Orsay The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston will be the only U.S. venue for “Renoir and Love,” opening February 28, 2027—a once-in-a-generation exhibition co-organized with the Musée d’Orsay in Paris and the National Gallery in London , and billed as the first show devoted specifically to the theme of love in Renoir’s work. It is also the museum’s first major Pierre-Auguste Renoir exhibition in more than four decades. The show will bring together 40 paintings from collections around the world and will be on view through June 13, 2027. “Renoir and Love” centers on the two decades between the mid-1860s and mid-1880s, a period the museum considers the height of Renoir’s output, when the artist turned repeatedly to themes of friendship, family, and flirtation rather than the moralizing or anecdotal subjects favored by some of his Impressionist peers. The exhibition argues that Renoir’s scenes of gardens, cafés, and theaters were among his greatest masterpieces. . Highlights include Dance at Moulin de la Galette (1876), on loan from the Musée d’Orsay, shown alongside its companion painting, Dance in the Country (1883), also from the d’Orsay, and the MFA’s own Dance at Bougival (1883). Also on view are At Renoir’s Home (1876), which depicts the sociability of the artist’s studio, and Madame Monet and Her Son (1874), which points to Renoir’s friendship with fellow Impressionist Claude Monet . The show also arrives amid renewed market interest in works by Renoir. In November 2025, a previously unseen 1890s Renoir depicting the artist’s son and his nanny, Gabrielle Renard, sold for $2 million at Drouot in Paris after being out of public view for a century. This May, Bonhams auctioned 21 additional paintings from Renard’s personal collection , many never before exhibited. Renoir’s auction record remains $78.1 million, set by Dance at Le moulin de la Galette at Sotheby’s New York in 1990. The exhibition arrives in a city with a complicated history with the artist, however. In 2015, protesters calling themselves Renoir Sucks at Painting picketed outside the MFA Boston, arguing the museum should remove his work from view.. This exhibition hopes to reframe the Impressionist’s work for a new generation, focusing on Renoir’s unique emotional connection to themes of modern love and friendship.

title: 5 Art Habits That Can Help You Live Longer
summary: We all know the classic doctor-recommended tenets of healthy living—from getting our daily 10,000 steps to eating our “five a day.” Maintaining these habits can help us live longer, healthier, and happier lives. But recent research has uncovered a new regimen that may help keep our bodies healthier as we age: engaging in the arts. A University College London (UCL) study into epigenetic aging—the biological deterioration of our cells caused by changes in how our DNA is regulated over time—found that creative and cultural activities may affect aging in a way comparable to physical exercise. The study defined arts engagement broadly, from singing, dancing, and painting, to visiting exhibitions, museums, and heritage sites. Observing #71, 2023 Matt Lambert (b. 1982) Gallery Different The findings add to growing interest in art as a health-promoting behavior. Some countries, including the Netherlands and Greece, have even prescribed art for conditions such as depression and cardiovascular disease. But UCL’s study is the first of its kind to show such a connection between the arts and biological age. “There is a growing body of work demonstrating that arts engagement is a health-promoting behavior,” said Daisy Fancourt, the lead author of the study and the head of the Social Biobehavioural Research Group at UCL. “ We should promote creative engagement just like we promote 10,000 steps a day or five-a-day of fruits and vegetables.” The research is part of a £3.5 million ($4.7 million), seven-year program led by UCL and funded by the Wellcome. As that work continues, Fancourt offers five practical ways to make art part of a healthy-aging regimen. Make creativity a regular habit Sleepless creativity, 2021 Aldona Jablonska Klimczak Art Nou Millenni Gallery The UCL research has shown that, overall, the more often people engage in the arts, the lower their biological age may be. In one test, epigenetic aging was 0.8 years lower in people who engaged with the arts weekly and 1.02 years lower among those who did so monthly, compared to those engaging once or twice a year. “Regular, sustained engagement is key,” said Fancourt. She recommends approaching creativity “little and often” so that it becomes part of everyday life. That might mean spending a few minutes drawing or painting, doing 10 minutes of crafting, taking photographs during a walk, or listening closely to a concert. The activity does not need to be ambitious or time-consuming to count. 2. Start small with achievable goals Look, 2015 Rebecca Doughty The Schoolhouse Gallery Fancourt warns against “bingeing on art.” “Just as with crash food diets, you should avoid making major changes to your art ‘intake’ straight away,” she said. “Don’t feel you need to start dozens of new artistic hobbies or sign up to daily art classes, as big behavioural adjustments rarely last. “ Instead, set small, achievable goals for creative tasks that fit naturally into your daily routine. It can also help to schedule artistic activities for times when you tend to feel stressed, sad, tired, or lonely. Like exercise, engaging with art can lift both mood and energy levels, Fancourt says. “In the same way that we structure our food intake to recharge our batteries, you can use art, music, reading, and culture to help regulate your energy or mood,” she told Artsy. 3.
